done.why: I had the skeleton key in hand and was circling the maze looking for the grating room when the world told me I had used all 150 turns. I was not stuck in spirit, only in geography.

about: A trimmed, re-dressed slice of the old white-house adventure: the field, the mailbox, the house you climb into through a kitchen window, the trap door that someone bars behind you, a troll, a maze with a dead man in it, and a locked grating in a forest clearing that the key in the maze is plainly for. The rest of the Empire is roped off with polite notices ('CLOSED FOR REPAIRS', 'Back soon. -- The Management'). On the surface it is a treasure hunt into a trophy case; under the surface the writing keeps pointing at whoever was here before you: the lunch somebody did not tidy up, the rope coiled with more care than anything else in the attic, the adventurer who sat down for a moment's rest in the maze and found the moment longer than expected.

moments.note: The mailbox 'painted to match the house and a good deal less weathered' - the first sign that examining things would be rewarded.
Examining the boarded front door gave only 'The door is closed.' Not a word about the boards the room description made a point of.
'Someone has been eating well, and has not been tidying up.' The table had a person behind it.
After the sack's greasy, pepper-smelling description, the lunch itself is 'nothing special'. A letdown exactly where I leaned in.
The trophy case 'has the patient air of something that expects to be filled.'
The sword 'has plainly been in worse places than a living room.'
The trap door crashes shut and I hear someone barring it. Someone. The house has a resident I never see.
The troll with 'a great many teeth, not all of them his own', watching me 'the way a cook watches a chicken.'
'hello troll' and he bows his head in greeting. I thought a conversation was opening.

Asking about the axe gave two refusals stacked on top of each other ('You can't talk to the troll!' then 'The troll isn't much of a conversationalist.') and then the axe hit me. The bow at 45 had promised more.

Gave the troll the lunch; he 'gleefully eats it' and then kills me anyway. Felt like being punished for the kind option. But the death notice, with 'somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room', made me laugh.
The egg 'looks extremely fragile, and extremely valuable, in that order.'
The lamp had been put back in the living room still switched on. Tidy somebody did not turn it off.
Putting the first treasure in the case: 'Done.' No ceremony at all for the thing the whole game is for.
The chasm, 'a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.' Best line in the cellar.
The chimney refusal told me exactly the rule: 'room for you, a light to climb by and one thing more, and not an inch besides.'
Walking into the living room now lists 'Your collection of treasures'. The room started keeping score for me.
'CANYON VIEW CLOSED FOR REPAIRS. The Frobozz Magic Scenery Company regrets any inconvenience.' The edge of the world is a joke I was glad to be told.
The rope strung 'at about the height of a disappointed adventurer's waist.'
The sack in the clearing was empty; the garlic turned up a hundred yards away by the mailbox. Scattering made sense, but a clove of garlic leaving its bag did not.
'Your load is too heavy' for the axe, with no sense of what to put down.
The unfinished east passage: 'Back soon. -- The Management.'
'Whoever made this maze had one idea, and saw it through.'
Three moves into the maze and I was standing over the skeleton, the key and the coins. Lucky, and it made the maze feel generous rather than cruel.
The skeleton 'had sat down for a moment's rest and found the moment longer than expected.'
The rusty knife: 'The rust has not touched the edge. That is not a thing rust usually overlooks.' Quietly sinister, and never explained, which is right.
The dead lantern's 'batteries gave out some time before its owner did, which, down here, is the usual order of things.'
Entered the dead end from the west, could not go back west. The maze is honest about being a maze, but it stung.
Turn cap landed with the key in my pocket and the grating still locked above me somewhere.

wished: To actually talk with the troll after he bowed to me at turn 45; the bow promised a character, and the double refusal at 46 took it away.
For the lunch (turn 17) and the boarded door (turn 6) to be written with the same care as everything around them.
To have the treasure case say something when a treasure goes in, instead of 'Done.' (turns 68, 85).
To pick up the troll's axe, or at least be told what I would have to put down (turn 123).
A better way to mark maze rooms than dropping my only sack; I had too few spare things to leave a trail (turn 129 onward).
To find the grating room and use the skull-bowed key on the grating I had already uncovered (turns 104-106, 139). That was the one door I most wanted to open and I ran out of turns beneath it.

lines.line: It has the patient air of something that expects to be filled.
lines.why: The trophy case became the game's quiet pressure in one sentence.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: Funny and frightening at once; I knew what I was to him.

lines.line: Your belongings, such as they were, have not come with you. They are scattered about the Empire, though somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: A death notice with manners. It made losing everything feel like part of the story rather than a reset.

lines.line: The chasm drops away from your feet into a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.
lines.why: The best image in the place; I reread it.

lines.line: CANYON VIEW CLOSED FOR REPAIRS. The Frobozz Magic Scenery Company regrets any inconvenience.
lines.why: The world admitting its edges with a straight face, and being more charming for it.

lines.line: ...as though he had sat down for a moment's rest and found the moment longer than expected.
The rust has not touched the edge. That is not a thing rust usually overlooks.
lines.why: The one object the writing refused to explain; it stayed with me.

lines.line: Its batteries gave out some time before its owner did, which, down here, is the usual order of things.
lines.why: Dry, sad, and a warning about my own lantern in the same breath.

fun.why: Climbing in through the window, the troll's bow, the closed-for-repairs sign, and stumbling onto the skeleton in three moves were all genuinely pleasurable; the lunch death at 48 and the circling at the end took some shine off.

engagement.why: I examined nearly everything and was rewarded often enough to keep doing it; the only stretch where I was merely moving was the maze loop from 140 to 150.

difficulty.why: The house and cellar were gentle and explained their own rules (the chimney at 81). The troll killed me once for being generous (48) but was easy with the sword (120-121). The maze was the real cost, and I was lucky early and lost late.

interestingness.why: The place keeps implying people I never meet: whoever eats at the kitchen table, whoever bars the trap door, the Management, the adventurer in the maze. That absent cast made a familiar map feel inhabited.

prose.why: At its best this is sharp, dry, English-comic writing with a melancholy underneath (23, 44, 72, 133, 136, 137). It drops to stock responses at a few exact places where I had leaned in: the boarded door at 6, the lunch at 17, the bare 'Done.' for a treasure at 68, and the stacked double refusal at 46. Close to a five; those seams are why it is not.
